title: Bit Manipulation: Count Set Bits
oneLiner: AND, OR, XOR, shifts -- the low-level operations bit-manipulation problems are built from, demonstrated by counting a number's 1 bits.
keyTakeaway: Bit tricks aren't magic -- they're five operations (AND &, OR |, XOR ^, NOT ~, shift <</>>) applied directly to a number's binary representation, often replacing a loop over an array or string with O(1)-per-bit work on a single integer. `n & 1` checks whether the lowest bit is set; `n >> 1` discards it and moves to the next one.
explanation: Five operations work directly on a number's bits: AND (&) gives 1 only where BOTH inputs have a 1; OR (|) gives 1 where EITHER input has a 1; XOR (^) gives 1 only where the inputs DISAGREE; NOT (~) flips every bit; and shifting (<< left, >> right) slides every bit over by one position, which is the same as multiplying or dividing by 2. To count how many 1 bits are in a number: check the lowest bit with `n & 1` (1 if it's set, 0 if not), add that to a running count, then `n >>= 1` to discard that bit and bring the next one into the lowest position -- repeat until n is 0. Two classic tricks worth knowing even though they're not needed for this exercise: `n & (n - 1)` clears the LOWEST set bit in one operation (Brian Kernighan's trick -- useful for a faster set-bit count, since it only loops once per 1-bit instead of once per bit total), and `(n & (n - 1)) == 0` for n > 0 checks whether n is a power of two (a power of two has exactly one set bit, so clearing it always leaves zero). Watch out for `n & 1` checking the LOWEST bit, not the highest -- it's easy to get the direction backward when reasoning about which end of the number you're inspecting.

visualizationSteps.message: 23 in binary is 10111. Check the lowest bit (n & 1), record it, shift right (n >>= 1), repeat until n is 0.
n & 1 = 1 -- this bit is set. count = 1. Shift right: n = 11.
n & 1 = 1 -- this bit is set. count = 2. Shift right: n = 5.
n & 1 = 1 -- this bit is set. count = 3. Shift right: n = 2.
n & 1 = 0 -- not set. count stays 3. Shift right: n = 1.
n & 1 = 1 -- this bit is set. count = 4. Shift right: n = 0.
n is now 0 -- done. 23 has 4 set bits.

recognitionSignals: The problem talks about binary representation, powers of two, or "set bits" directly.
You need to check, toggle, or count individual bits of a number rather than treat it as one opaque value.
A brute-force approach would convert the number to a string or array of digits to inspect it -- bit operations usually do the same job in O(1) extra space.
gotchas: `n & 1` checks the LOWEST (rightmost) bit, not the highest -- easy to get backward when reasoning about which end of the number you're looking at.

Right-shifting a NEGATIVE number can sign-extend (fill with 1s, not 0s) depending on the language/type -- a loop assuming "shift until n == 0" can spin forever on negative input if that's not accounted for.

`n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest SET bit, not the lowest bit period -- it's a no-op shortcut specifically because subtracting 1 flips every trailing 0 (and the lowest 1) up to and including that lowest set bit.
confusableWith: Bitmask subset enumeration (Bits: All Subsets by Counting Bitmasks) also manipulates bits, but there each bit means "is this element included in the subset" -- same five operations, completely different meaning attached to each bit.

complexity.note: Shifting right once per bit visits about log₂ n bits (the number of bits in n). Brian Kernighan's n & (n-1) trick runs once per SET bit instead, which can be fewer.
